item.title: Kanda Matsuri — Guide
item.description: The Kanda Matsuri, centred on Kanda Myojin Shrine, is one of Tokyo’s three great Shinto festivals (alongside the Sanja and Sanno matsuri) and dates back to the Edo period, when it was celebrated as a display of prosperity under the Tokugawa shogunate. The festival’s grandest events are held in full scale only in odd-numbered years (alternating with the Sanno Matsuri), over several days in mid-May. Its highlight is a spectacular day-long procession that winds for kilometres through the Kanda, Nihonbashi and Otemachi districts of central Tokyo — a long parade featuring people in Heian-era court costume, priests on horseback, musicians, dancers and floats, followed on another day by around a hundred mikoshi (portable shrines) carried energetically through the streets to the shrine.

item.title: Sanja Matsuri — Guide
item.description: The Sanja Matsuri, held over a weekend in mid-May at Asakusa Shrine beside Senso-ji Temple, is one of Tokyo’s three great Shinto festivals and among the largest, wildest and most exciting in the city. Honouring the three founders of Senso-ji, it draws around 1.5 to 2 million people over three days and centres on the boisterous parading of mikoshi — ornate portable shrines believed to house the deities. Around a hundred mikoshi from the local neighbourhoods, plus three huge main shrines, are hoisted onto the shoulders of teams of chanting, tightly-packed bearers and carried, bouncing and swaying, through the crowded streets in an electric, high-energy atmosphere.

item.title: Sumiyoshi Matsuri Guide: Osaka's Great Summer Purification Festival
item.description: Held at the end of summer, the Sumiyoshi Matsuri is the grand festival of Sumiyoshi Taisha, one of Osaka’s oldest and most important shrines — and it traditionally closes the city’s festival season each year. Centred on purification and renewal, its highlights are the solemn Nagoshi-no-harae rite, in which participants pass through a great reed ring to cleanse themselves of the year’s impurities, and a boisterous procession that carries a giant mikoshi (portable shrine) across the Yamato River to a related shrine in Sakai.
